PBL Module 1 Report

Octopuses or Octopi:
Predicting the Future of Latin and Greek Plurals

The Decline of Classical Plurals, The Rise of Simplified Plurals
CHEN YIMING 2022390235  ·  LIN HENGJUN 2023390205
YEO SOJIN 2025390064  ·  LEE CHAERIN 2022390203

Section 1Introduction

For centuries, educated English speakers were expected to produce classical plurals for words borrowed from Greek and Latin — octopi rather than octopuses, formulae rather than formulas, phenomena rather than phenomenons. These forms served as markers of scholarly literacy and linguistic tradition.

Yet the dominant trend in contemporary English is clear: simplified plural forms are steadily displacing their classical counterparts. Words like stadiums, octopuses, and formulas have already overtaken their classical alternatives in general usage. Where classical plurals do persist — as with criteria, phenomena, and analyses — they survive primarily because academic and professional discourse continues to treat them as the only acceptable standard. Even this resistance has its limits, however. Cases like indices/indexes and appendices/appendixes show that simplified forms can gain acceptance even within formal registers, suggesting that no domain is entirely immune to the regularizing trend.

This report analyzes a selected set of Greek and Latin-origin nouns using corpus-based usage data to examine the rate and direction of these shifts, identify the factors driving them, and offer projections for which forms are likely to be treated as standard by 2040. It concludes with practical recommendations for lexicographers and education policymakers.

Section 2Research Questions

  • Which nouns are shifting toward regularized English plurals (for example, -s or -es), and which retain their classical forms? Why does this difference occur?
  • What patterns emerge when usage data is examined across registers, disciplines, and time periods?
  • Which plural forms are most likely to be treated as standard by 2040?

Section 4Corpus-Based Usage Analysis and Rate Comparison

This section examines usage data from the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) and Google Books Ngram Viewer for a selected set of Greek and Latin-origin nouns. The findings reveal three distinct patterns of change, each representing a different stage in the regularization process.

Category 1: Rapid Regularization

These words have shifted decisively toward simplified English plurals in contemporary usage.

Stadiums / Stadia

In COCA, stadiums accounts for 2,102 occurrences compared to just 122 for stadia, representing approximately 95% of all usage. Ngram data reinforces this trajectory: stadia was actually the more frequent form until the mid-twentieth century, but stadiums overtook it around the 1960s and has widened the gap ever since.

Focuses / Foci

The simplified form dominates even more decisively here. COCA records 13,863 instances of focuses against just 601 for foci, giving the regularized form a 96% share. The classical plural foci survives mainly in scientific and mathematical contexts, where it retains a precise technical meaning.

Formulas / Formulae

COCA shows 3,154 occurrences of formulas versus 547 for formulae, placing the simplified form at approximately 85% of total usage. While formulae still appears occasionally in academic and scientific writing, formulas has become the clear default across all other registers.

Octopuses / Octopi

With 355 occurrences in COCA versus 100 for octopi, octopuses holds roughly 78% of usage. Although octopi remains culturally familiar — and is often cited in popular debates about "correct" plurals — it is worth noting that octopi is itself a hypercorrection, applying a Latin plural rule to a word of Greek origin. The regularized form is now the more widely accepted standard.

The shift in this category has been driven largely by the fact that these words are commonly used outside of specialist discourse. They appear frequently in journalism, everyday conversation, and popular writing, where speakers naturally default to the productive English -s/-es rule rather than recalling a classical inflection.

Category 2: Classical Retention

At the opposite end of the spectrum, the words in this category show virtually no movement toward regularization.

Criteria / Criterions

COCA records 23,812 instances of criteria against just 15 for criterions — a ratio of over 99.9% to less than 0.1%. The classical form is so dominant that the regularized alternative barely registers as a variant at all.

Phenomena / Phenomenons

A similar pattern holds here, with 8,342 occurrences of phenomena versus only 54 for phenomenons in COCA, representing a 99.4%-to-0.6% split. Ngram data confirms that phenomenons has remained a flat line near zero across the entire 1800–2022 period.

Analyses / Analysises

This pair shows the most extreme resistance to regularization. COCA records 20,511 occurrences of analyses and just 1 for analysises. The regularized form is essentially nonexistent.

Bases / Basises

The pattern here is absolute: 13,751 occurrences for bases and zero for basises in COCA. No regularization has occurred whatsoever.

The words in this category share a critical feature: they are used predominantly in academic and professional writing. In COCA, 3,709 of phenomena's 8,342 occurrences appear in academic texts, making it the dominant register by a wide margin. In these contexts, the classical plural is not simply preferred but expected, reinforced by disciplinary conventions, style guides, and peer review processes. The regularized forms are so rare that using them in formal writing would likely be perceived as errors rather than acceptable alternatives.

Category 3: Coexistence Across Registers

These word pairs complicate any simple narrative about regularization by showing that both classical and simplified forms can coexist as legitimate variants, even within academic writing.

Indices / Indexes

In COCA, indices appears 2,620 times and indexes 1,997 times, yielding a roughly 57%-to-43% split. Unlike the clear dominance seen in the first two categories, both forms are in widespread active use. What makes this pair particularly noteworthy is the register distribution: indices leads heavily in academic writing (1,952 vs 659), but indexes outperforms it in news (263 vs 47) and magazine writing (338 vs 90), suggesting a functional split based on audience and context.

Appendices / Appendixes

A similar pattern emerges here, with 352 occurrences for appendices versus 98 for appendixes in COCA — approximately 78% to 22%. While the classical form still leads, the simplified alternative holds a meaningful share of usage, including within formal writing contexts.

These cases challenge the assumption that classical plurals survive only because of academic gatekeeping. Instead, they show that both forms can coexist as legitimate variants, with register and audience determining which is chosen.

What Explains the Variation?

The rate of regularization appears to be governed primarily by how closely a word is tied to academic and specialist usage. Words that have entered the general vocabulary — like stadium and octopus — regularize quickly because most speakers encounter them in everyday contexts where classical morphology offers no communicative advantage. Words that remain concentrated in scholarly writing — like phenomenon and criterion — retain their classical plurals because academic norms actively enforce them. The middle cases, like index, suggest that when a word serves both general and specialist functions, a dual-plural system can emerge, with each form occupying its own register niche.

Section 52040 Usage Projections

Based on our COCA results, we expect many of the nouns we examined to continue moving toward regular English plural forms by 2040. In several cases, the regular forms already appear more frequently than the classical ones, which suggests that they are becoming the more common choice in present-day English. This trend is most clearly shown in the first category, where regular plural forms consistently dominate over their classical alternatives. Similar tendencies can be seen in examples such as stadiums/stadia, focuses/foci, formulas/formulae, and octopuses/octopi. If this pattern continues, regular plurals will likely become even more established in general usage.

However, our results also show that this shift is not completely uniform. The second and third categories suggest that not all Greek- and Latin-origin nouns are following the same path of change. In the second category, classical plural forms remain clearly dominant, as seen in examples such as analyses/analysises, bases/basises, phenomena/phenomenons, and criteria/criterions. In the third category, the pattern is more mixed: classical forms still remain strong, but the gap between the two forms is narrower, as in indices/indexes and appendices/appendixes. These patterns show that some nouns continue to resist full regularization, especially in more specialized or convention-based contexts.

For that reason, by 2040, regular plurals will probably become the main standard for many nouns in everyday English, education, and general reference use. At the same time, some classical forms are likely to remain important where they are still strongly supported by convention, meaning, or field-specific usage. Overall, the future pattern is likely to be stronger regularization for many nouns, but continued competition or partial retention of classical plurals for others.

Section 6Recommendations for Dictionaries and Education Policy

Based on the projected trends toward increasing regularization alongside the continued presence of classical forms, both dictionaries and educational policies should adopt a balanced and context-sensitive approach.

For Lexicographers Both regularized and classical plural forms should be included as standard entries, rather than treating one as strictly correct and the other as incorrect. Dictionaries should clearly label each form according to its typical usage context (e.g., general vs. academic) and, where possible, indicate relative frequency. When one form is becoming dominant, it may be presented as the primary entry, with the alternative listed as a secondary or variant form. This approach reflects actual language use and ongoing change more accurately.
For Curriculum Designers Regularized plural forms in -s/-es should be taught as the default standard for general communication. However, widely used classical plurals such as criteria, phenomena, and analyses should still be explicitly taught, especially in academic contexts. Rather than presenting these forms as fixed rules, instruction should emphasize variation and context, helping learners understand when and why different forms are used.

Overall, both dictionaries and educational practices should move away from rigidly prescriptive norms and instead reflect the dynamic nature of English pluralization, recognizing both the trend toward regularization and the continued role of classical forms in specific domains.

Section 7Conclusion

This report set out to examine how the pluralization of Greek and Latin-origin nouns is shifting in contemporary English, and the findings point to a consistent, data-supported narrative. The overarching trend is one of regularization: simplified plural forms ending in -s/-es are steadily gaining ground across general usage. Words like stadiums, octopuses, formulas, and focuses have already decisively overtaken their classical counterparts, and corpus data from both COCA and Google Books Ngram Viewer confirms that this shift has been accelerating since the mid-twentieth century.

Yet regularization is not a uniform process. A significant group of nouns — including phenomena, criteria, analyses, and bases — continue to resist simplification almost entirely. What sustains these classical forms is not tradition alone but the active reinforcement of academic and professional discourse, where they remain the expected and often the only acceptable standard. As long as these disciplinary conventions persist, full regularization of such words remains unlikely.

At the same time, the existence of a third pattern — seen in pairs like indices/indexes and appendices/appendixes — reveals that the boundary between classical and simplified usage is not as rigid as it may appear. Even within formal and academic registers, regularized alternatives have gained legitimate standing, suggesting that no domain is entirely closed to the broader forces of language change.

Looking ahead to 2040, regular plurals will likely become the default standard for most Greek and Latin-origin nouns in everyday English, education, and general reference. Classical forms will persist where convention, precision, or disciplinary norms demand them, but increasingly as recognized variants rather than sole standards. Dictionaries and educational policies should reflect this reality by presenting both forms with clear contextual guidance, moving away from rigid prescriptivism and toward an approach that mirrors how English is actually used and evolving.

In short, the question is no longer whether English will simplify its borrowed plurals — it already is. The more productive question is which forms will hold, where they will hold, and how institutions can best adapt to a language that, as always, refuses to stand still.
